paras: The killing of James Truss was the fatal stabbing of a Black man at Desoto, Mississippi, on a Saturday night in late September or early October 1881. Truss died within minutes of a stab wound to the neck, and five men, four white and one Black, were said to have been involved. The killing is known from a single brief in a Memphis paper's column of Mississippi news.

According to the Memphis Daily Appeal of October 8, 1881, Truss, whom it described as an "inoffensive and peaceable colored man," was killed at Desoto "last Saturday night" by a stab in the neck. He lived only a few minutes after he was stabbed. The item did not say where in Desoto the stabbing took place, what led to it, or who struck the blow.
Relaying what "is said," the paper named five men as "concerned in the matter": Burt McRee, Young Nealy, Cook Johnson and Cooper Morris, identified as white, and Royal Evans, identified as "colored."
No report of an arrest, inquest, indictment or trial of any of the five men appears in the coverage.

The Appeal printed the killing without a headline as one paragraph of its "Mississippi Matters" column, between a note on a lynching threat against a prisoner in Sharkey County and a list of delegates to a river convention. The column was dominated by political notes for the state campaign and short notices of deaths and accidents, and the Truss item carried no comment beyond its description of the victim as peaceable. It gave the race of the victim and of each man said to be concerned, but it stated no motive and attributed the names only to report.
No other white paper's account was found, and the Black press of the period is not represented in the available sources.
